bib.title: Combining Models (Chapter 14 of Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning)

question: How can several models be combined, by averaging, boosting, input-dependent selection (trees) or probabilistic mixtures, to beat a single model?
contributions: Distinguishes Bayesian model averaging from model combination (14.1)
Committees and bagging with bias-variance argument (14.2)
AdaBoost derived as sequential exponential-error minimisation (14.3)
CART trees: growing, pruning, impurity measures (14.4)
Conditional mixtures: linear, logistic, mixtures of experts, HME (14.5)

results.claim: If member errors are zero-mean and uncorrelated, committee error is 1/M of the average member error.
results.setup: Regression, M models y_m=h+eps_m, sum-of-squares, assumptions (14.12)-(14.13)
results.quote: ECOM = 1 M EAV.
results.note: Text extraction prints eq 14.14 as 'ECOM = 1 M EAV.' (fraction 1/M split across lines).

results.claim: In practice errors are highly correlated so the gain from bagging-style averaging is generally small, though E_COM <= E_AV always holds.
results.setup: Committee of M bootstrap-trained models, sum-of-squares; the bound uses Jensen (Exercise 14.3)
results.quote: In practice, the errors are typically highly correlated, and the reduction in overall error is generally small.

results.claim: Bagging: train M copies on M bootstrap data sets and average their predictions.
results.setup: Regression, y_COM = (1/M) sum y_m(x)
results.quote: This procedure is known as bootstrap aggregation or bagging (Breiman, 1996).

results.claim: AdaBoost starts every point at weight 1/N, sets alpha_m = ln((1-eps_m)/eps_m), multiplies weights of misclassified points by exp(alpha_m), and predicts sign(sum alpha_m y_m).
results.setup: Two-class, t in {-1,+1}, base classifier trained on weighted data
results.quote: Each data point is given an associated weighting parameter wn, which is initially set 1/N for all data points.

results.claim: Boosting can work with weak learners only slightly better than random.
results.setup: Qualitative
results.quote: Boosting can give good results even if the base classiﬁers have a performance that is only slightly better than random, and hence sometimes the base classiﬁers are known as weak learners.

results.claim: AdaBoost demo uses 30 data points from toy set with decision stumps, shown through m=150 learners.
results.setup: Fig 14.2 snapshots at m = 1, 2, 3, 6, 10, 150; base learner a threshold on one input (decision stump)
results.quote: The AdaBoost algorithm is illustrated in Figure 14.2, using a subset of 30 data points taken from the toy classiﬁcation data set shown in Figure A.7.

results.claim: AdaBoost is sequential minimisation of exponential error E = sum exp(-t_n f_m(x_n)), with f_m = 1/2 sum alpha_l y_l; this reproduces the alpha and weight updates.
results.setup: Earlier learners and coefficients held fixed; minimise over alpha_m and y_m only
results.quote: Friedman et al. (2000) gave a different and very simple interpretation of boosting in terms of the sequential minimization of an exponential error function.

results.claim: Learning-theory generalisation bounds that motivated boosting are too loose to be useful; real performance is much better.
results.setup: Qualitative
results.quote: However, these bounds turn out to be too loose to have practical value, and the actual performance of boosting is much better than the bounds alone would suggest.

results.claim: Population minimiser of expected exponential error is half the log-odds, 1/2 ln p(t=1|x)/p(t=-1|x), motivating the sign rule.
results.setup: Variational minimisation over all y(x)
results.quote: which is half the log-odds.

results.claim: Exponential loss grows exponentially for large negative t*y, cross-entropy only linearly, so exponential is much less robust to outliers; it is not a log likelihood and does not extend to K>2 classes.
results.setup: Cross-entropy ln(1+exp(-yt)) rescaled by ln 2 to pass through (0,1)
results.quote: whereas the exponential error function grows exponentially with |ty|.

results.claim: Boosting with sum-of-squares error reduces to fitting each new learner to residuals t_n - f_{m-1}(x_n); absolute deviation makes it robust to outliers.
results.setup: Additive model (14.21), regression
results.quote: simply involves ﬁtting each new base classiﬁer to the residual errors tn−fm−1(xn) from the previous model.

results.claim: CART grows a tree greedily by exhaustive search over region, variable and threshold, leaf prediction = local mean (regression).
results.setup: Regression, sum-of-squares; optimal structure search is combinatorially infeasible
results.quote: a greedy optimization is generally done by starting with a single root node, corresponding to the whole input space, and then growing the tree by adding nodes one at a time.

results.claim: Grow a large tree with a minimum-leaf-size stop rule, then prune with C(T)=sum Q_tau + lambda|T|, lambda by cross-validation.
results.setup: Because no single split may reduce error even when later splits would
results.quote: it is common practice to grow a large tree, using a stopping criterion based on the number of data points associated with the leaf nodes, and then prune back the resulting tree.

results.claim: For classification growth, cross-entropy and Gini beat misclassification rate; pruning generally uses misclassification rate.
results.setup: Node impurity Q_tau(T)
results.quote: The cross entropy and the Gini index are better measures than the misclassiﬁcation rate for growing the tree because they are more sensitive to the node probabilities.

results.claim: Tree structure is very sensitive to the training data; splits are axis-aligned and hard, so regression is piecewise constant.
results.setup: Qualitative; cites Hastie et al.
results.quote: a small change to the training data can result in a very different set of splits (Hastie et al., 2001).

results.claim: Mixture of two linear regressions fitted by EM: converged log likelihood -3.0 versus -27.6 for a single linear regression.
results.setup: Synthetic 1-input data set, mixture of 2 lines, EM 50 iterations (Fig 14.8), beta initialised to reciprocal of true variance of targets
results.quote: This gives a log likelihood value of −3.0.
results.note: Single linear regression log likelihood is -27.6 (same caption); Fig 14.8 centre = 30 EM iterations, right = 50. Data set size is not stated.

results.claim: EM for mixture of linear regressions: responsibilities (14.37), pi_k = mean responsibility (14.38), weighted least squares w_k=(Phi^T R_k Phi)^-1 Phi^T R_k t (14.42), 1/beta = weighted mean squared residual (14.44).
results.setup: Common noise precision beta across K components
results.quote: wk = ΦTRkΦ−1 ΦTRkt.

results.claim: Mixture of logistic regressions: M step has no closed form and is solved with IRLS per component on data weighted by gamma_nk.
results.setup: Binary classification, EM
results.quote: Note that the M step does not have a closed-form solution and must be solved iteratively using, for instance, the iterative reweighted least squares (IRLS) algorithm.

results.claim: Mixture of experts: gating functions pi_k(x) (e.g. linear softmax) times experts p_k(t|x); linear experts fit by EM with IRLS in the M step.
results.setup: Jacobs et al. 1991; Jordan and Jacobs 1994 for EM+IRLS
results.quote: This is known as a mixture of experts model (Jacobs et al., 1991) in which the mixing coefﬁcients πk(x) are known as gating functions and the individual component densities pk(t|x) are called experts.

results.claim: Bayesian model averaging assumes a single model generated the whole data set; model combination lets different points come from different components.
results.setup: Contrast: mixture of Gaussians (combination) vs Gaussian-mixture vs Cauchy-mixture models p(h) (averaging); posterior p(h|X) concentrates as N grows
results.quote: in Bayesian model averaging the whole data set is generated by a single model.

limits: Gives no experiments on real data; only toy illustrations (Fig 14.2, 14.8, 14.9, 14.10) with sizes mostly unstated.
Committee gain 1/M relies on uncorrelated errors, which the text says rarely holds.
Does not cover random forests, gradient-boosting details beyond residual fitting, shrinkage, or stacking; published 2006 so predates XGBoost-style practice.
Boosting generalisation bounds called too loose; exponential loss not robust to outliers and no K>2 extension; HME not treated in detail.
Trees: unstable, axis-aligned, hard splits, piecewise-constant regression.
practices: Average models trained on bootstrap data sets (bagging) to cancel variance; use low-bias models (p. 655-656).
Use weak, simple base learners such as decision stumps in AdaBoost (p. 657-659).
Grow a large tree with a minimum-leaf-size rule then prune with cost-complexity C(T), choosing lambda by cross-validation (p. 665).
Grow classification trees with cross-entropy or Gini, prune with misclassification rate (p. 666).
To make boosting robust to outliers in regression, use absolute deviation rather than squared error (p. 662-663).
Use EM with weighted least squares or IRLS for mixture models; each M-step is a weighted fit of a single model (p. 668-672).

terms.definition: combination of models by averaging their predictions
bootstrap aggregation: average of models trained on M bootstrap data sets
training multiple models in sequence where the error function for one depends on the performance of previous models
base classifier only slightly better than random
decision tree with a single node: threshold on one input
classification and regression trees (Breiman et al., 1984)
p(t|x)=sum pi_k(x) p_k(t|x) with gating functions and experts
multilevel gating; each component is itself a mixture of experts; probabilistic version of decision trees
sum over models h of p(X|h)p(h); one model generates the whole data set

code.snippet: w_n^(1)=1/N; for m=1..M: fit y_m minimising J_m=sum w_n^(m) I(y_m(x_n)!=t_n); eps_m=sum w I / sum w; alpha_m=ln((1-eps_m)/eps_m); w_n^(m+1)=w_n^(m) exp{alpha_m I(y_m(x_n)!=t_n)}; Y_M(x)=sign(sum alpha_m y_m(x))
